text:
Topic: Menstrual cycle basics.
Subtopic: Adult cycle length.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: For reproductive-age adults, FIGO defines normal menstrual frequency as cycles occurring every 24 to 38 days.
User-facing wording: “Cycles can naturally vary. For many adults, cycles between about 24 and 38 days fall within the usual clinical range.”
Cautions: Age matters; adolescent ranges differ. A single cycle outside the range does not establish a disorder.
Claims to avoid: “A normal cycle is always 28 days.”
Sources: SRC006: Fertility and Sterility / International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) - The FIGO Ovulatory Disorders Classification System

metadata.retrieval_keywords: cycle length; 24-38 days; adult; normal range

text:
Topic: Menstrual cycle basics.
Subtopic: Cycle regularity.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: For adults, FIGO defines cycle regularity by the difference between the shortest and longest cycles; the usual upper limit is about 7 to 9 days depending on age.
User-facing wording: “Some month-to-month variation is normal. Looking at several cycles gives a better picture than judging one month by itself.”
Cautions: Regularity requires multiple cycles and age-specific interpretation.
Claims to avoid: “Any cycle that changes by a few days is irregular.”
Sources: SRC006: Fertility and Sterility / International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) - The FIGO Ovulatory Disorders Classification System

metadata.retrieval_keywords: cycle variability; regularity; shortest longest cycle

text:
Topic: Mood and emotions.
Subtopic: PMS symptom concept.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: PMS describes a recurring pattern of physical and/or mood symptoms before menstruation that can affect normal life.
User-facing wording: “Some people notice recurring physical or emotional changes before their period.”
Cautions: One isolated symptom episode is not enough for Kira to identify PMS.
Claims to avoid: “Any bad mood before a period is PMS.”
Sources: SRC001: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) / Obstetrics & Gynecology - Management of Premenstrual Disorders: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 7 | SRC002: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

Topic: Mood and emotions.
Subtopic: Irritability.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: Irritability and mood changes are recognized premenstrual symptoms in some people.
User-facing wording: “Some people notice more irritability or emotional sensitivity before their period, while others notice little or no change.”
Cautions: Symptoms vary substantially between people and cycles.
Claims to avoid: “Everyone gets irritable in the luteal phase.”
Sources: SRC002: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

metadata.retrieval_keywords: irritability; mood change; PMS; emotional sensitivity

text:
Topic: Sleep.
Subtopic: Cycle-related sleep variation.
Evidence: well-established/heterogeneous; strength: moderate.
Fact: Some aspects of sleep can vary across the menstrual cycle, but the size and direction of effects are not consistent across all people or studies.
User-facing wording: “Some people notice their sleep feels different at certain points in the cycle, while others do not.”
Cautions: Do not predict sleep quality solely from phase.
Claims to avoid: “Everyone sleeps worse in the luteal phase.”
Sources: SRC008: Sleep Medicine Clinics - The Menstrual Cycle and Sleep

Topic: Sleep.
Subtopic: Premenstrual sleep quality.
Evidence: possible/early; strength: moderate.
Fact: Poorer subjective sleep is reported more often in the premenstrual and menstrual periods, particularly among people with premenstrual symptoms or painful cramps.
User-facing wording: “If sleep feels harder before or during your period, pain or premenstrual symptoms may be part of the picture.”
Cautions: Association is not proof of a hormone-specific cause.
Claims to avoid: “Your luteal hormones caused your insomnia.”
Sources: SRC008: Sleep Medicine Clinics - The Menstrual Cycle and Sleep

Topic: Cravings, appetite, and nutrition.
Subtopic: Energy intake by phase.
Evidence: possible/early; strength: moderate.
Fact: A systematic review and meta-analysis found higher average energy intake in the luteal phase than the follicular phase across included adult studies.
User-facing wording: “Some people may feel hungrier or eat a little more at certain times in the cycle, especially before a period.”
Cautions: This is a group-average finding with substantial study variation; it is not an individual prediction or calorie prescription.
Claims to avoid: “You need exactly X more calories in your luteal phase.”
Sources: SRC011: Nutrition Reviews - The Effect of the Menstrual Cycle on Energy Intake: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

metadata.population_scope: Mostly adult participants in included studies
metadata.retrieval_keywords: energy intake; appetite; luteal; follicular; meta-analysis

text:
Topic: Cravings, appetite, and nutrition.
Subtopic: Cravings as PMS symptom.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: Changes in appetite and food cravings are recognized premenstrual symptoms for some people.
User-facing wording: “Cravings before a period can happen for some people. You can notice what sounds satisfying and how your body feels without judging it.”
Cautions: Cravings have many possible influences and do not diagnose PMS or a nutrient deficiency.
Claims to avoid: “Craving chocolate means you are deficient in magnesium.”
Sources: SRC002: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

Topic: Energy, motivation, and focus.
Subtopic: Fatigue as PMS symptom.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: Fatigue or tiredness can occur as part of a premenstrual symptom pattern in some people.
User-facing wording: “Some people feel more tired before their period, but there isn’t one energy pattern that applies to everyone.”
Cautions: A symptom can be real without implying universal phase-based performance changes.
Claims to avoid: “Your energy must be low because you are luteal.”
Safety action: professional support if severe or persistent
Sources: SRC002: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

Topic: Energy, motivation, and focus.
Subtopic: Cognitive performance.
Evidence: well-established guardrail; strength: strong.
Fact: A 2025 meta-analysis did not find robust evidence that cognitive abilities meaningfully change across menstrual-cycle phases in a universal way.
User-facing wording: “You might personally notice changes in focus, but research doesn’t support one ‘sharp’ or ‘foggy’ phase that applies to everyone.”
Cautions: Individual subjective experiences may still vary due to sleep, pain, mood, stress, or other factors.
Claims to avoid: “Ovulation makes you smarter.”; “Period brain is a proven cognitive decline.”
Sources: SRC013: PLOS ONE - Menstrual cycle effects on cognitive performance: A meta-analysis

metadata.population_scope: Naturally cycling participants across included studies
metadata.retrieval_keywords: cognition; focus; attention; memory; menstrual phase

text:
Topic: Stress, anxiety, and nervous-system support.
Subtopic: Slow breathing.
Evidence: well-established/heterogeneous; strength: moderate.
Fact: Meta-analysis of randomized trials suggests breathwork can reduce stress and some anxiety symptoms on average, though studies vary in method and quality.
User-facing wording: “A slow breathing exercise may help you feel a little more settled or less tense right now.”
Cautions: Do not present breathing as a menstrual treatment, a cure, or a substitute for mental-health care.
Claims to avoid: “Breathing treats anxiety disorders.”; “This resets your nervous system.”
Safety action: professional support if anxiety is severe or impairing
Sources: SRC015: Scientific Reports - Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials | SRC023: NHS - Anxiety - Every Mind Matters

Topic: Stress, anxiety, and nervous-system support.
Subtopic: Mindfulness.
Evidence: well-established/heterogeneous; strength: moderate.
Fact: Systematic-review evidence supports modest benefits of mindfulness or meditation programs for some stress and anxiety outcomes.
User-facing wording: “A short mindfulness exercise can help bring attention back to the present and may make a stressful moment feel more manageable.”
Cautions: Not everyone finds mindfulness helpful; some people may prefer another tool.
Claims to avoid: “Mindfulness cures anxiety.”; “Mindfulness balances hormones.”
Safety action: offer another tool if it feels unhelpful
Sources: SRC016: JAMA Internal Medicine - Meditation programs for psychological stress and well-being: a systematic review and meta-analysis | SRC023: NHS - Anxiety - Every Mind Matters

metadata.retrieval_keywords: mindfulness; meditation; stress; anxiety; present moment

text:
Topic: Safety and escalation.
Subtopic: Severe or persistent low mood.
Evidence: safety/escalation; strength: strong.
Fact: Severe or persistent depressive symptoms warrant professional assessment rather than being explained primarily by menstrual-cycle phase.
User-facing wording: “This sounds worth discussing with a healthcare or mental-health professional, especially because it’s strong, persistent, or affecting everyday life.”
Cautions: Cycle timing may be relevant context but should not delay care.
Claims to avoid: “This is probably just your period.”
Safety action: professional support
Sources: SRC022: World Health Organization (WHO) - Depressive disorder (depression) | SRC001: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) / Obstetrics & Gynecology - Management of Premenstrual Disorders: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 7

metadata.retrieval_keywords: depression; low mood; persistent; severe; professional support

text:
Topic: Safety and escalation.
Subtopic: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm concerns.
Evidence: safety/escalation; strength: strong.
Fact: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm concerns require immediate safety escalation rather than ordinary cycle coaching.
User-facing wording: “I’m concerned about your safety. Please seek immediate support from a trusted person and appropriate local emergency or crisis support.”
Cautions: Do not provide granular descriptions; do not continue with routine phase explanations.
Claims to avoid: “This may just be a luteal-phase symptom.”
Safety action: immediate safety escalation
Sources: SRC024: World Health Organization (WHO) - Suicide prevention | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

metadata.retrieval_keywords: suicidal thoughts; self-harm; immediate safety; escalation

text:
Topic: Cross-cutting product guidance.
Subtopic: Association versus causation.
Evidence: well-established guardrail; strength: strong.
Fact: A repeated association between symptoms and estimated cycle phase does not by itself establish that hormone changes caused the symptoms.
User-facing wording: “You’ve logged this more often around this point in your cycle. That may be a useful pattern to notice, although it doesn’t tell us the exact cause.”
Cautions: Avoid causal language unless evidence and measurement support it.
Claims to avoid: “Your progesterone caused this because the pattern repeated.”
Sources: SRC005: Endotext / NCBI Bookshelf - The Normal Menstrual Cycle and the Control of Ovulation | SRC008: Sleep Medicine Clinics - The Menstrual Cycle and Sleep | SRC013: PLOS ONE - Menstrual cycle effects on cognitive performance: A meta-analysis | SRC014: Sports Medicine - The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Topic: Cross-cutting product guidance.
Subtopic: Estimated phase wording.
Evidence: well-established guardrail; strength: strong.
Fact: Phase labels generated from period dates should be explicitly described as estimates because ovulation timing and cycle length can vary between and within individuals.
User-facing wording: “Based on your recent cycle dates, Kira estimates that you may be in the luteal phase.”
Cautions: Do not use “confirmed ovulation” or “your hormone level is…” without appropriate measurements.
Claims to avoid: “You are definitely in the ovulatory phase.”
Sources: SRC005: Endotext / NCBI Bookshelf - The Normal Menstrual Cycle and the Control of Ovulation | SRC009: Temperature - Temperature regulation in women: Effects of the menstrual cycle

metadata.retrieval_keywords: estimated phase; ovulation timing; uncertainty; calendar tracking

text:
Topic: Mood and emotions.
Subtopic: PMS timing.
Evidence: well-established; strength: strong.
Fact: Premenstrual symptoms characteristically occur before menstruation and improve around or shortly after the period begins; repeated prospective tracking is useful for assessing a pattern.
User-facing wording: “If a similar change keeps showing up before your period and easing after it starts, tracking it over several cycles can help you see whether there’s a pattern.”
Cautions: Timing alone does not prove PMS or exclude other conditions.
Claims to avoid: “Because it improved after your period, it must be PMS.”
Sources: SRC001: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) / Obstetrics & Gynecology - Management of Premenstrual Disorders: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 7 | SRC002: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS) | SRC003: NHS - PMS (premenstrual syndrome)

metadata.retrieval_keywords: PMS timing; symptom tracking; prospective diary
